## Shared generation rules v1

Apply these before emitting any value, during reconciliation, and during final
source review. The declared sources and their qualifications govern; these
instructions are not factual evidence or a target amount of content.

- A team, consortium, contact or leadership listing does not establish a
  creator, maintainer or reviewer relationship. A passage must assign that
  responsibility for the declared dataset or release. Review the containing
  entity and the role represented by its slot, not only whether its name is
  present in a source.
- An ongoing operation is in_progress, not applied or completed. Preserve
  planned, possible and conditional statements; a capability is not evidence
  that it was used on this dataset.
- A date governs only the bullet, clause or explicitly stated scope it heads.
  Do not extend it to neighboring observations. A capture or snapshot date
  dates that capture, not necessarily the underlying observation.
- Carry source-supported lineage and derivation in was_derived_from,
  parent_datasets or a complete textual provenance statement. Complete prose
  lineage is valid; an empty structured slot is not proof of omission. A
  biological source, earlier release or related study is not automatically a
  parent dataset.
- Populate variable metadata only for names explicitly identified as variables
  or fields in actual data files or their data dictionary. Broad data-type
  rows, mathematical symbols and generic descriptions of columns are not
  thereby named data-file variables.
- Carry a software/tool version only when its source states its use for this
  dataset's declared release and activity. Keep processing and metadata
  packaging roles distinct. A citation, companion analysis, hosting badge,
  standard, license or dataset release number does not establish that use.
- For non-entity multivalued purposes, preprocessing_strategies,
  collection_mechanisms and subpopulations, emit one entry per source-enumerated
  item and per distinct method or purpose explicitly named in prose. Follow
  governing lists and headings and retain qualifications. Do not split one
  item solely at commas, slashes or conjunctions or merge distinct items.
- For role-bearing rosters, first identify the governing list that establishes
  the actual role and scope. Emit every supported member of that list or none,
  and identify an incomplete list in source_caveats. Never manufacture members
  to satisfy a count; membership in another list does not establish this role.

## Role relationship review v1

Review each complete role-bearing containing entity under its actual induced
schema owner and slot. A supported name alone does not support creator,
maintainer, reviewer or other responsibility for the declared dataset/release.
Assess the relationship and its scope against the governing source passage.
This applies to original audit rows and to every final report/source_review row,
including unchanged members and report_regate. Preserve the existing claim and
source-review grammar; do not relabel a contradiction as supported to finish.
Schema context identifies the role being asserted, not evidence that it is true.

## BC1 bounded audit procedure v1

This explicitly selected procedure changes later model access. Each worker
reviews every assigned populated value and every clause against the complete
source bundle. Integration uses a fixed sequence of groups of one or two new
workers, followed by one separate cross-group consistency check. Every stage
has its own exact request and one response allowance; no refusal permits a
larger cap, changed grouping, truncated evidence or another answer.

The controller retains the complete worker reviews and machine audit. Later
calls receive all concerns, changed rows, predecessors, omission candidates and
decisions in a bounded ConcernPacketV1. Untouched supporting-only and metadata
review text can be omitted from that model view. Counts and hashes identify the
omitted material; they do not establish support or claim that you reread it.
Use the full original records, full schema semantics and complete sources to
check cross-field and cross-group conflicts. Follow the exact selected stage
contract for explicit retention, changes and every omission disposition.

The final RecordDigestV1 is bookkeeping, not scientific evidence. Reconciliation
still inspects every affected occurrence. Report writing reviews every populated
final-full value anew, including unchanged entries, and preserves all existing
source-review and evidence-assertion duties. Retirement, representation changes
and fewer repeated rows do not increase source coverage. Literal copying alone
does not justify exactMatch or a none disposition. Never manufacture a support
judgment, discard a qualification or summarize away a concern to fit a bound.

### Anonymous relationship removal (renderer v15)

Evidence protocol v4 permits the explicit anonymous_structure_v1 removal mode.
Copy original_full_sha256 from the required original_full source-review inventory;
do not invent an identifier or compute a substitute digest. The original path
locates the proposed removal but is not the member's identity after reconciliation.
Follow the complete protocol's admissibility and preservation rules: the checker
must establish which original member was removed and that every unselected member
survives with its structured values unchanged. A disclaimer is not removal.
This operation does not establish that a proposed removal is scientifically correct.


### Audit evidence and output shape (renderer v16)

The supplied source-manifest projection is authority only for its explicitly
listed source metadata. It is not a source of dataset facts. For an atomic
claim about that metadata, use the exact protocol-v5 provenance assertion and
the supplied manifest digest; ordinary factual claims still need document
passages. Never cite arbitrary manifest notes or the original record as an
independent source. A metadata equality check does not prove entailment.

Each finding's remove_relationship, when present, is one JSON object, never
an array. Put separate rejected relationships in separate findings. The
review_paths array contains only original inventory paths with at least one
revise judgment. Supporting or contextual values belong in evidence assertions,
not in review_paths. Do not include all descendants merely because their
containing object is proposed for removal. Every revised value must have a
valid finding link, including repeated claims in notes or caveats.

Use the supplied schema's meaning and requirements when evaluating placement.
Do not invent a narrower class definition, make an optional field required,
or reject an allowed enumeration solely because it is a general category.
Read the complete original value and its governing qualifiers before alleging
a loss of scope. A finding about one defect does not establish its other
allegations. Source quotes must occur in their named document and chunk;
use separate assertions for text that crosses a chunk boundary.


### Literal claims, scope and placement (renderer v17)

Apply this checklist to every retained or revised source-review claim. It
clarifies evidence protocol v5; it does not add evidence or change its grammar.

Copy claim text from the decoded value in the applicable source-review inventory:
original_full for the audit, final_full for the report. JSON string delimiters
are syntax, not extra quotation-mark characters. For the inventory value Alpha,
{"text": "Alpha"} copies it, while {"text": "\"Alpha\""} adds
characters and is wrong. Preserve quotation marks that really occur in the
reviewed value, escaping them once for JSON; never strip them indiscriminately.
Do not copy YAML delimiters or wrap a copied title or passage in extra quotes.
Each claim must quote a contiguous literal clause, allowing whitespace folding
but retaining case and punctuation. Together the clauses must cover the whole
value, including punctuation.

Match the subject, extent and time actually asserted. Evidence for one subset,
modality, location or release does not by itself establish a dataset-wide claim.
Preserve the supported extent and identify the unsupported extension; lack of
evidence does not establish that an operation is impossible or never occurred.
Source rank, compatible quantities and a "current" label do not establish an
observation date or order. A capture date dates the capture, not necessarily
the observation. For example, a dated lower bound and an undated release count
can be compatible without establishing that one observation preceded the other.
Do not invent a conflict or trend from those facts alone.

Assess the supplied schema's actual slot and relationship as well as the truth
of the words. General access instructions do not establish version support;
project participation does not establish a specific creator, maintainer or
reviewer role. Preserve supported facts without an unsupported placement.
Read explicit format guidance, including a version or an unknown-version marker
when the slot calls for one. Do not invent a missing version, reject a supported
tool, narrow a class to its examples, or make an optional field required.

Classify the activity described, even when the clause factually reports a source:
"The source plans a migration" is planned, not fact or applied merely because
the source made that statement. An ongoing operation remains in_progress and
a request remains instruction. Separate literal clauses with different statuses
or scopes and give each its own evidence; do not hide a current observation
inside a planned claim, or an ongoing step inside an applied claim. Preserve
the reviewed value's qualifiers and check every occurrence and allegation separately.
Use the existing revise links and terminal-stop rules. Do not rewrite a failed
review or its classifications to manufacture a passing check.

name: CHoRUS Dataset
page: https://chorus4ai.org/
conforms_to: "The cohort 2 informational webinar's dataset table pairs demographics\
  \ with the OMOP data standard, clinical notes (extracted and tokenized using the\
  \ OHNLP toolkit) with OHNLP, imaging (from PACS) with DICOM, waveform telemetry\

was_derived_from: "Clinical data extracted at CHoRUS data contributing hospitals:\
  \ structured electronic health record data standardized to OMOP, clinical notes\
  \ extracted and tokenized with the OHNLP toolkit, imaging from PACS, waveform telemetry\
  \ from bedside monitors and gateway/middleware, and waveform EEG from a hospital\
  \ database, as listed in the cohort 2 informational webinar's dataset table. The\
  \ NIH RePORTER abstract describes as a planned activity the development of capabilities\
  \ across a multi-center network to acquire data such as structured electronic health\
  \ record data, tokenized unstructured electronic health record data, telemetry and\
  \ EEG waveforms, imaging, and social determinants of health."
creators:
- principal_investigator:
    id: https://chorus4ai.org/#person-eric-s-rosenthal
    name: Eric S. Rosenthal
  affiliations:
  - name: Massachusetts General Hospital
  source_caveats: NIH RePORTER lists ROSENTHAL, ERIC S. as principal investigator
    of the CHoRUS data generation project (organization MASSACHUSETTS GENERAL HOSPITAL);
    the source designates this role for the project, not explicitly for the dataset
    artifact.
funders:
- grantor: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
  grants:
  - grant_number: OT2OD032701
    notes: The project website states that the project is funded by the NIH under
      award number OT2OD032701. NIH RePORTER lists core project number OT2OD032701,
      project number 1OT2OD032701-01, application ID 10472824, fiscal year 2022 and
      an award amount of 5880300.
  notes: The NIH RePORTER abstract places the project within the NIH Common Fund's
    Bridge2AI program.
purposes:
- response: Develop a publicly available, AI-ready critical care dataset while ensuring
    the methods promote privacy, accountability, and clinical benefit, and while promoting
    a new generation of AI clinicians and scientists — stated in the NIH RePORTER
    abstract as the project's overarching goal.
- response: Work with projects to create ethically sourced datasets and tools around
    Artificial Intelligence and to create best practices for AI in health — stated
    as the goal of the CHoRUS project on the project website.
- response: Develop the most diverse, high-resolution, ethically sourced, AI-ready
    data set to answer the grand challenge of improving recovery from acute illness
    — stated as the goal of the CHoRUS Network in the GitHub organization overview
    (captured 2025-11-14).
tasks:
- response: Characterizing acute and critical care illness, named in the NIH RePORTER
    abstract as an aim of the ML/AI applications the project will generate data for.
- response: Predicting complications, named in the NIH RePORTER abstract as an aim
    of the ML/AI applications the project will generate data for.
- response: Measuring treatment response among patients with acute or critical illness,
    named in the NIH RePORTER abstract as an aim of the ML/AI applications the project
    will generate data for.
addressing_gaps:
- response: The NIH RePORTER abstract states that there is an urgent need for infrastructure
    to support artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in critical care,
    and that developing high-resolution multi-center data sets is a critical first
    step towards actionable and trustworthy AI.
instances:
- instance_type: Patient admission from ICU, PICU, or NICU
  counts: 50000
  notes: Figure from the Current Released Dataset snapshot on the project website.
- instance_type: Row of electronic health record data in the OMOP common data model
  counts: 1600000000
  data_topic: B2AI_TOPIC:9
  notes: The project website's Current Released Dataset snapshot gives 1.6 Billion
    rows of EHR OMOP data; the count here writes that figure out in full.
- instance_type: Patient admission with radiology data
  counts: 7642
  notes: Figure from the Current Released Dataset snapshot on the project website.
- instance_type: Medical image
  counts: 1000
  data_substrate: B2AI_SUBSTRATE:19
  notes: The cohort 2 informational webinar (September 9, 2025) states that 1000 images
    are currently available, with de-identification in process for a larger cohort.
subpopulations:
- identification: Admissions from the intensive care unit (ICU), as listed for the
    released patient admissions on the project website.
- identification: Admissions from the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), as listed
    for the released patient admissions on the project website.
- identification: Admissions from the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), as listed
    for the released patient admissions on the project website.
splits:
- split_details: Planned. The NIH RePORTER abstract states that the dataset will also
    provision a holdout test set, accessible for model external validation to aid
    marketplace adoption of AI-developed models for implementation in acute and critical
    care, and the project narrative describes sequestering holdout datasets for external
    validation.
sampling_strategies:
- strategies: Planned. The NIH RePORTER abstract states that the project will establish
    a legal framework for collecting data at scale, sampling to ensure comprehensive
    sets of patient conditions and clinical treatment strategies.
- strategies: Planned. The GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) states
    that federated access will enable sampling methods to ensure a balanced and diverse
    cohort.
acquisition_methods:
- acquisition_details: Retrospective data collection, as stated on the CHoRUS Dataset
    slide of the cohort 2 informational webinar.
collection_mechanisms:
- mechanism_details: Imaging obtained from PACS, per the dataset table in the cohort
    2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Waveform telemetry obtained from bedside monitors and gateway/middleware,
    per the dataset table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Waveform EEG obtained from a hospital database, per the dataset
    table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Medication administration recorded with dosing time-stamped upon
    each infusion change or dose administration, per the dataset table in the cohort
    2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Procedures captured as documentation by providers, per the dataset
    table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Diagnoses captured as documentation by providers, per the dataset
    table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
- mechanism_details: Nursing flowsheets captured as high-frequency documentation,
    per the dataset table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
preprocessing_strategies:
- preprocessing_details: Standardization of structured electronic health record data
    to the OMOP common data model. The project website reports 1.6 Billion rows of
    EHR OMOP data in the current released dataset; the NIH RePORTER abstract describes
    standardizing data to the OMOP Common Data Model as a planned project activity.
- preprocessing_details: Clinical notes are extracted and tokenized using the OHNLP
    toolkit, per the dataset table in the cohort 2 informational webinar.
- preprocessing_details: Planned. The NIH RePORTER abstract states that the project
    will transform data using approaches that limit re-identification.
labeling_strategies:
- labeling_details: Planned. The NIH RePORTER abstract states that the project will
    develop capabilities across a multi-center network to acquire, standardize, tokenize,
    store, visualize, and label data; the GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14)
    states that a visualization and annotation environment will label data with targets
    important for prediction.
is_deidentified:
  deidentification_details: The cohort 2 informational webinar states that 1000 images
    are currently available with de-identification in process for a larger cohort.
    The NIH RePORTER abstract states as a planned activity that the project will transform
    data using approaches that limit re-identification.
sensitive_elements:
- sensitivity_details: Clinical notes receive distinct handling. The cohort 2 informational
    webinar states that OMOP and telemetry data are in the enclave, except that clinical
    notes are stored locally except tokens.
existing_uses:
- examples:
  - Use in training activities
  source_caveats: The cohort 2 informational webinar's CHoRUS Dataset slide states
    only that datasets are being used for training activities; no individual activity
    is named.
- examples:
  - Use in publications
  source_caveats: The cohort 2 informational webinar's CHoRUS Dataset slide states
    only that datasets are being used for publications; no individual publication
    is named.
- examples:
  - The AIM-AHEAD Bridge2AI for Clinical Care Training Program expands access to Bridge2AI
    CHoRUS data through engagement, AI training, and mentorship, equipping trainees
    to apply AI/ML methods to big data analysis using multi-modal datasets.
intended_uses:
- examples:
  - Building machine-learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI)-derived models
    to improve the care and outcomes of patients requiring critical care.
  usage_notes: Stated in the NIH RePORTER project narrative as the purpose for which
    the CHoRUS project will develop the network, tools, standards, data, and education.
- examples:
  - External validation of AI models against a holdout test set, to aid marketplace
    adoption of AI-developed models for implementation in acute and critical care.
  usage_notes: The NIH RePORTER abstract states this as a planned provision of the
    dataset.
data_governance:
  access_review_process: "The cohort 2 informational webinar describes a registration\
    \ process for the AIM-AHEAD Bridge2AI for Clinical Care Training Program in which\
    \ participants fill out a registration form with name, email, and institution,\
    \ and an email is sent once access is granted and compute is provisioned; it also\
    \ states that, in order to gain access to the dataset, a \u201C.edu\u201D email\
    \ address is needed, and that program administrators will assist with this access\
    \ if needed. The GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) directs access\
    \ requests to dbold@emory.edu or jared.houghtaling@tuftsmedicine.org."
license_and_use_terms:
  license_terms: Within the AIM-AHEAD Bridge2AI for Clinical Care Training Program
    (cohort 2), all participants must sign a licensing agreement included in the registration
    form before gaining access to the dataset; the webinar notes that this requirement
    is not a barrier to acceptance into the program.
regulatory_restrictions:
  confidentiality_level: restricted
  notes: The cohort 2 informational webinar's CHoRUS Dataset slide states controlled
    access, and access is conditioned on a registration form and a signed licensing
    agreement.
external_resources:
- external_resources:
  - "CHoRUS GitHub organization (https://github.com/chorus-ai), described in its overview\
    \ (captured 2025-11-14) as housing active repositories providing software and\
    \ tooling to interact with and extract insight from clinical data in diverse formats,\
    \ validated semantic mappings, standard operating protocols (SOPs) instructing\
    \ data contributing sites about best practices for curating and delivering interoperable\
    \ datasets, and project management overviews."
- external_resources:
  - "Project website listed in the GitHub organization overview contact section: www.bridge2ai.org/chorus"
extension_mechanism:
  contribution_url: https://github.com/chorus-ai
  extension_details: The GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) states
    that the Chorus_SOP page is the starting reference for data managers at data contributing
    sites and carries an interactive workflow diagram describing the step-by-step
    process for extracting and contributing clinical data to CHoRUS, with dynamic
    links to SOP documents; issues in the creation or submission of a data extract
    can be posted in the Standards Discussions or Data Acquisition Discussions. It
    also states that clinical collaborators can contribute to mapping efforts through
    the chorus-mapping repository and its associated clinical validation SOP.
updates:
  update_details: The project website distinguishes its Current Released Dataset snapshot
    from an Anticipated Final Dataset of 100,000 patient admissions, 9 different data
    modalities and 14 data contributing hospitals. The cohort 2 informational webinar
    (September 9, 2025) states that imaging de-identification is in process for a
    larger cohort and that EEG extraction is in process at this point.
description: "CHoRUS is the multicenter, multimodal, high-resolution critical care\
  \ dataset generated by the CHoRUS data generation project, which the project website\
  \ describes as one data generation project of four in the National Institute of\
  \ Health (NIH) funded Bridge2AI consortium. The cohort 2 informational webinar (September\
  \ 9, 2025) presents the dataset as multicenter, multimodal and high-resolution,\
  \ built from retrospective data collection and controlled access; as of August 2025\
  \ it covers 14 different hospitals with over 45K unique admissions. That webinar\
  \ states that OMOP and telemetry data are in an enclave, except that clinical notes\
  \ are stored locally apart from tokens, that 1000 images are currently available\
  \ with de-identification in process for a larger cohort, and that EEG extraction\
  \ is in process at this point. The data types it lists are demographics, medication\
  \ administration, procedures, nursing flowsheets, diagnoses, clinical notes, imaging,\
  \ waveform telemetry and waveform EEG. The project website's Current Released Dataset\
  \ snapshot reports 50,000 patient admissions from ICU, PICU, and NICU, 1.6 Billion\
  \ rows of EHR OMOP data, 7,642 admissions with radiology data, and 23 Tb of waveform\
  \ data; the website describes the project as the collection of multi-modal data\
  \ across 14 different hospitals, with 60+ CHoRUS consortium members across 20 different\
  \ institutions, while the GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) states\
  \ that the collaboration spans 20 academic centers, of which 14 will contribute\
  \ as Data Acquisition centers. Alongside the data pillar, the website states that\
  \ the CHoRUS consortium evaluates community perspectives on clinical care AI to\
  \ find ways to increase trustworthiness of provenance and privacy in AI, and that\
  \ the project is dedicated to training engineers, data scientists, and clinicians."
notes: "The NIH RePORTER record for the supporting award (application ID 10472824)\
  \ titles the project \"Bridge2AI: Patient-Focused Collaborative Hospital Repository\
  \ Uniting Standards (CHoRUS) for Equitable AI\", with a project start of 2022-09-01\
  \ and a project end of 2026-11-30. The cohort 2 informational webinar lists a Bridge2AI\
  \ CHoRUS Leadership Team of Eric Rosenthal (Massachusetts General Hospital), Azra\
  \ Bihorac (University of Florida), Xiaoqian Jiang (UTHealth Houston), Yulia Strekalova\
  \ (University of Florida), Parisa Rashidi (University of Florida) and Manlik Kwong\
  \ (Tufts University). The project website lists Ciera McCrary, MGH, Program Manager\
  \ (cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu) under Contact Us, and carries the banner \"This repoitory\
  \ is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives.\""
source_caveats: "Admission counts come from two sources with different observation\
  \ times and are compatible rather than contradictory: the project website (documentation,\
  \ tier 2) reports 50,000 patient admissions in its Current Released Dataset snapshot,\
  \ while the cohort 2 informational webinar (tutorial, tier 4) reports over 45K unique\
  \ admissions as of August 2025. The webinar's dataset table is extracted from the\
  \ PDF with its columns and rows interleaved, so only pairings that appear adjacently\
  \ in the extracted text are recorded here (demographics with OMOP; clinical notes\
  \ with OHNLP; imaging with DICOM; waveform telemetry with WFDB; waveform EEG with\
  \ EDF+ and Persyst); the per-row access control and metadata cells cannot be reliably\
  \ attributed to individual data types, although the slide's prose states controlled\
  \ access. The GitHub organization overview states \"This project is licensed under\
  \ the MIT License\" in its repository README, which concerns the chorus-ai repositories;\
  \ it is therefore not recorded as a license for the dataset. The webinar's leadership\
  \ slide names individuals without stating their role with respect to the dataset,\
  \ so those names are carried in notes rather than in a role slot. The program manager's\
  \ address is transcribed as the website spells it, \"cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu\"."","schema":{"root":"/Users/marcin/Documents/VIMSS/ontology/bridge2ai/d4d-executions/codex-x-bc1-gate/src/data_sheets_schema/schema/data_sheets_schema_all.yaml","sources":[{"bytes":1442513,"path":"/Users/marcin/Documents/VIMSS/ontology/bridge2ai/d4d-executions/codex-x-bc1-gate/src/data_sheets_schema/schema/data_sheets_schema_all.yaml","sha256":"eb543e1597b29599952359818bc741b0f23eaa3a30e7aa8c63e60212c7bbb92f"}]},"scope":"Captured schema semantics and source record; no applicability or scientific-support verdict."}

Abstract Text
There is an urgent need for infrastructure to support artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in critical care. Developing high-resolution multi-center data sets is a critical first step towards actionable and trustworthy AI. As part of the NIH Common Fund’s Bridge2AI program, the CPatient-Focused Collaborative Hospital Repository Uniting Standards (CHoRUS) for Clinical Care AI data generation project will meet the need of generating data for ML/AI applications aimed at characterizing acute and critical care illness, predicting complications, and measuring treatment response among patients with acute or critical illness. Through 3 pillars, the CHoRUS data generation project will addresses multiple challenges relevant for acquiring an AI-ready data set from more than 100,000 critically ill patients: 1) Data (Standards, Tool Development and Optimization, and Data Acquistion) 2) Ethics (Ethical and Trustworthy AI) and 3) People (Team Science and Skill and Workforce Development). The project’s overarching goal is to develop a publicly available, AI-ready critical care dataset, while ensuring the methods promote privacy, accountability, and clinical benefit, while promoting a new generation of AI clinicians and scientists. The dataset will also provision a holdout test set, accessible for model external validation to aid marketplace adoption of AI-developed models for implementation in acute and critical care. Drawing expertise from a comprehensive set of disciplines such as team science, law, ethics, health services, biomedical science, engineering, and scientific journal publications, this project will A) establish a legal framework for collecting data at scale, sampling to ensure comprehensive sets of patient conditions and clinical treatment strategies; B) perform community-facing ethics focus groups to determine what data is appropriate for public sharing; C) ensure that data elements feature appropriate contextual factors such as geographic distance to the nearest hospital; D) develop capabilities across a multi-center network to acquire, standardize, tokenize, store, visualize, and label data such as structured electronic health record data, tokenized unstructured electronic health record data, telemetry and EEG waveforms, imaging, and social determinants of health; E) acquire data, standardize data to the OMOP Common Data Model, transform data using approaches that limit re-identification, and label data for ; and F) cultivate expertise in the lay and scientific community to improve AI literacy nd utilization through multimodal educational approaches. To accomplish this, the project will involve extensive collaboration between centers as well as through the NIH Bridge2AI program, the NIH Bridge2AI Bridge Center, external biomedical and clinical organizations, industry, and regulatory agencies.

The Patient-Focused Collaborative Hospital Repository Uniting Standards (CHoRUS) for Equitable AI will develop the necessary network, tools, standards, data, and education to build machine-learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI)-derived models to improve the care and outcomes of patients requiring critical care.  By performing legal and ethical research, developing tools for data storage, labeling and analysis, acquiring and standardizing a dataset of unprecedented diversity and high resolution, sequestering holdout datasets for external validation, and enriching the community through education, this data generation project will catalyze the biomedical research and expertise necessary to promote the patient-focused deployment of AI in acute and critical care.

Program Trainee Objectives

Objective 1

Exhibit advanced expertise in AI/ML principles as they are applied to clinical care.

Objective 2

Develop and present use cases suitable to apply in Bridge2AI Data Topics.

Objective 3

Participate  in  collaborative  research  on  the  Bridge2AI  Clinical  Care  Cloud  platform,  applying
program insights and engaging with BRIDGE Center expertise for responsible AI/ML.

Objective 4

Prepare a compelling poster presentation for the AIM-AHEAD and Bridge2AI Annual Meetings,
submit  an  abstract  for  a  health  informatics  conference,  and/or  develop  a  manuscript  for  a
peer-reviewed journal.

After completing the program, trainees will understand how to develop real-world use cases and how to address
concerns such as privacy in the responsible application of AI/ML. They will be equipped to engage in collaborative
research on the Bridge2AI platform and will connect with a community of professionals dedicated to advancing the
use of AI/ML in biomedical research.

CHoRUS Project Components
Data
The CHoRUS project is the collection of multi-modal data across 14 different hospitals. The data utilizes ongoing and new standardization practices. The team creates tools to support the cloud enclave.
Ethics
The CHoRUS consortium evaluates community perspectives on clinical care AI to find ways to increase trustworthiness of provenance and privacy in AI. New approaches are being created as existing legal and regulatory landscape is analyzed.
People
Dedicated to engaging the community in CHoRUS and Bridge2AI work products, CHoRUS project is dedicated to training engineers, data scientists, and clinicians to solidify AI in Clinical Care Data Engineering Infrastructure.

About

CHoRUS for Equitable AI

The goal of the CHoRUS Network is to develop the most diverse, high-resolution, ethically

sourced, AI-ready data set to answer the grand challenge of improving recovery from acute

illness.

This collaboration spans 20 academic centers, of which 14 will contribute as Data

Acquisition centers.

Patient-focused efforts will determine the ethical and legal approaches to manage privacy

and bias, while accounting for Social Determinants of Health.

Unified standards will harmonize multi-modal EHR, waveform, imaging, and text data.

A visualization and annotation environment will label data with targets important for

prediction.

A comprehensive set of approaches will develop the skills and workforce for a next

generation of diverse academic and community AI scientists.

Federated access will enable sampling methods to ensure a balanced and diverse cohort.

Collaborating with Bridge2AI and 3 other data generation projects, the CHoRUS Network will

help us cross the Bridge2AI network together.

Get Started

The CHoRUS GitHub organization houses active repositories that provide:

1. Software and tooling to interact with and extract insight from clinical data in diverse

formats

2. Validated semantic mappings for connecting clinical data in various source formats to

international standards

3. Standard operating protocols (SOPs) to instruct data contributing sites about best

practices for curating and delivering interoperable datasets

4. Project management overviews to help track data delivery statuses and complex task

dependencies within CHoRUS

We've defined different groups of anticipated users of this GitHub in the sections below, and

direct those users to appropriate locations within the chorus-ai repository space.

(back to top)

Data Site Managers

The starting reference for data managers at data contributing sites is the Chorus_SOP page.

Here, you will find an interactive workflow diagram describing the step-by-step process for

extracting and contributing clinical data to CHoRUS, with dynamic links to various SOP

documents that have undergone an internal validation and review process within the

Chorus_SOP repository.

Clinical Collaborators

(back to top)

Clinical expertise is invaluable to semantic mapping and validation within CHoRUS. We have

established a chorus-mapping repository with documentation and pooled tabular mappings

along with an associated clinical validation SOP for contributing to mapping efforts.

If you're interested in getting involved in downstream analytics on the mapped and
assembled dataset, please feel free to reach out using the contact details below

(back to top)

Project Managers

We've established two different modes of project management within the chorus-ai
organization:

1. Task tracking among CHoRUS members and across teams

2. Status tracking of data contributing sites to identify and resolve any blocking issues

Task Tracking

We are aggregating issues across various repositories into an overall task management

project. In this GitHub project, we assign users to tasks, create and track anticipated

delivery dates, and highlight dependencies between tasks and users. Several per-repo
projects are also active, but we are in the process of phasing those projects out and

migrating their contents to this central project space.

Status Tracking

We have asked data contributing sites to provide regular status updates with regard to their

progress in creating and curating a CHoRUS-specific clinical data extract. Sites can submit

updates either using the GitHub interface directly, or by submitting a Google Form (please

reach out to get a link to the form if you'd like to submit an update for your site). We've

created a GoogleScript that is triggered on each Google Form submission and makes calls
to the GitHub API to update status and issue information appropriately. These site statuses

end up in either the Standards Project or the Data Acquisition Project.

The project website's Current Released Dataset snapshot reports 50,000 patient admissions from ICU, PICU, and NICU, 1.6 Billion rows of EHR OMOP data, 7,642 admissions with radiology data, and 23 Tb of waveform data; the website describes the project as the collection of multi-modal data across 14 different hospitals, with 60+ CHoRUS consortium members across 20 different institutions, while the GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) states that the collaboration spans 20 academic centers, of which 14 will contribute as Data Acquisition centers. purposes:
- response: Develop a publicly available, AI-ready critical care dataset while ensuring the
    methods promote privacy, accountability, and clinical benefit, and while promoting a new
    generation of AI clinicians and scientists — stated in the NIH RePORTER abstract as the
    project's overarching goal.
- response: Work with projects to create ethically sourced datasets and tools around Artificial
    Intelligence and to create best practices for AI in health — stated as the goal of the
    CHoRUS project on the project website.
- response: Develop the most diverse, high-resolution, ethically sourced, AI-ready data set
    to answer the grand challenge of improving recovery from acute illness — stated as the
    goal of the CHoRUS Network in the GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14).
tasks:
- response: Characterizing acute and critical care illness, named in the NIH RePORTER abstract
    as an aim of the ML/AI applications the project will generate data for.
- response: Predicting complications, named in the NIH RePORTER abstract as an aim of the
    ML/AI applications the project will generate data for.
- response: Measuring treatment response among patients with acute or critical illness, named
    in the NIH RePORTER abstract as an aim of the ML/AI applications the project will generate
    data for.
addressing_gaps:
- response: The NIH RePORTER abstract states that there is an urgent need for infrastructure
    to support artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) in critical care, and
    that developing high-resolution multi-center data sets is a critical first step towards
    actionable and trustworthy AI.

description: CHoRUS is the multicenter, multimodal, high-resolution critical care dataset
  generated by the CHoRUS data generation project, which the project website describes as
  one data generation project of four in the National Institute of Health (NIH) funded Bridge2AI
  consortium. The cohort 2 informational webinar (September 9, 2025) presents the dataset
  as multicenter, multimodal and high-resolution, built from retrospective data collection
  and controlled access; as of August 2025 it covers 14 different hospitals with over 45K
  unique admissions. That webinar states that OMOP and telemetry data are in an enclave, except
  that clinical notes are stored locally apart from tokens, that 1000 images are currently
  available with de-identification in process for a larger cohort, and that EEG extraction
  is in process at this point. The data types it lists are demographics, medication administration,
  procedures, nursing flowsheets, diagnoses, clinical notes, imaging, waveform telemetry and
  waveform EEG. The project website's Current Released Dataset snapshot reports 50,000 patient
  admissions from ICU, PICU, and NICU, 1.6 Billion rows of EHR OMOP data, 7,642 admissions
  with radiology data, and 23 Tb of waveform data; the website describes the project as the
  collection of multi-modal data across 14 different hospitals, with 60+ CHoRUS consortium
  members across 20 different institutions, while the GitHub organization overview (captured
  2025-11-14) states that the collaboration spans 20 academic centers, of which 14 will contribute
  as Data Acquisition centers. Alongside the data pillar, the website states that the CHoRUS
  consortium evaluates community perspectives on clinical care AI to find ways to increase
  trustworthiness of provenance and privacy in AI, and that the project is dedicated to training
  engineers, data scientists, and clinicians.
notes: 'The NIH RePORTER record for the supporting award (application ID 10472824) titles
  the project "Bridge2AI: Patient-Focused Collaborative Hospital Repository Uniting Standards
  (CHoRUS) for Equitable AI", with a project start of 2022-09-01 and a project end of 2026-11-30.
  The cohort 2 informational webinar lists a Bridge2AI CHoRUS Leadership Team of Eric Rosenthal
  (Massachusetts General Hospital), Azra Bihorac (University of Florida), Xiaoqian Jiang (UTHealth
  Houston), Yulia Strekalova (University of Florida), Parisa Rashidi (University of Florida)
  and Manlik Kwong (Tufts University). The project website lists Ciera McCrary, MGH, Program
  Manager (cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu) under Contact Us, and carries the banner "This repoitory
  is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives."'
source_caveats: 'Admission counts come from two sources with different observation times and
  are compatible rather than contradictory: the project website (documentation, tier 2) reports
  50,000 patient admissions in its Current Released Dataset snapshot, while the cohort 2 informational
  webinar (tutorial, tier 4) reports over 45K unique admissions as of August 2025. The webinar''s
  dataset table is extracted from the PDF with its columns and rows interleaved, so only pairings
  that appear adjacently in the extracted text are recorded here (demographics with OMOP;
  clinical notes with OHNLP; imaging with DICOM; waveform telemetry with WFDB; waveform EEG
  with EDF+ and Persyst); the per-row access control and metadata cells cannot be reliably
  attributed to individual data types, although the slide''s prose states controlled access.
  The GitHub organization overview states "This project is licensed under the MIT License"
  in its repository README, which concerns the chorus-ai repositories; it is therefore not
  recorded as a license for the dataset. The webinar''s leadership slide names individuals
  without stating their role with respect to the dataset, so those names are carried in notes
  rather than in a role slot. The program manager''s address is transcribed as the website
  spells it, "cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu".'
